title: Coverage limits and next evidence for the Eucharistic book-stage chronology
scope: Coverage crosswalk of the canonical candidate inventories and stage dossiers at the input hashes below. This audit reconciles their declared evidence, witnesses and gaps; it creates no stages, transitions, local reception claims or text-completion claims.

count_semantics.warning: These count different objects. Western trajectories include composite and overlapping discovery buckets. Presentation groups are display categories. Neither candidate linkage nor a dossier certifies complete coverage.

findings: Retain every existing coverage row, including index-only and unresearched local uses, alongside selected new dossiers.
A missing unique Church edition is not itself a gap: one source book may serve several communities. Missing exact book identity and local reception evidence are real gaps.

Slovak reception of the shared Lviv 1905 book and later source-language exemplars is source-described. Official translation approvals are now identified; exact source copies and dated local implementation remain separate questions.

Albanian and Macedonian exact received source-language books remain unidentified. A Macedonian translation approval is recorded without establishing its exemplar. Bulgarian Vulgata audience evidence still does not establish actual adoption.
Roman Greek, Ruthenian and Vulgata, Coptic and Ge’ez, and the separate East/West Syriac Catholic lines must not become single family-wide evolutionary chains.
Publication, approval, effective implementation and modern editorial publication dates are separate. Candidate witness bounds below are not stage-validity intervals.
A component, complementary volume or appended calendar does not represent an entire successive Eucharistic book.
No assigned new dossier covers the full early sacramentary corpus or all Sarum/York/Hereford/continental diocesan and monastic trajectories.

Selected local-use, canonical-order and Slavonic Roman stages now resolve to their own dossiers. Composite discovery rows retain unmapped communities and incomplete periods; no dossier supplies whole-book text completeness.
Complete native constituents count as partial book coverage. Recorded book states, optional rules and complementary volumes do not create a complete missal or authorize text inheritance.

sources.title: Usuarium 48: Missale Barcinonense
sources.inspection: Read bibliographic fields, fragment warning and contents index. Catalogue gives 1498, Didacus de Gumiel, Biblioteca de Catalunya Inc. 46-Fol.; surviving span begins at Holy Saturday and ends at 25 January.
sources.limitations: Catalogue metadata only. Original page images not inspected. Holding-platform link failed with cache miss.

sources.title: Usuarium 55: Missale Salmanticense
sources.inspection: Read bibliographic fields and contents index: 1533, Ioannes Junta, BU Salamanca BG/18686; title page at catalogue image 5, decree/calendar at 7 and colophon at 609. Also read the beginning of the linked conspectus, without verifying against images.
sources.limitations: Original page images and decree not inspected. Holding-platform handle failed with cache miss. No revision established.

sources.title: Usuarium 57: Missale Hispalense
sources.inspection: Read bibliographic fields and contents index: 1565, Ioannes Gutiérrez, BU Sevilla A Res. 10/1/06; title at catalogue image 14, preface/decree at 16, colophon at 682 (328v).
sources.limitations: Original images uninspected; linked Spanish heritage record returned HTTP 429. The catalogue's decree label is not an independent authentication of a normative act.

sources.title: Usuarium 60: Missale Toletanum
sources.inspection: Read bibliographic fields, explicit Roman-use classification and contents index: 1551, Bartholomaeus Fraenus, BM Lyon SJ L 013/14. Catalogue locates title/decree at images 5–6 and final colophon at 679; linked Google Books landing page was accessible.
sources.limitations: Original pages not inspected. Keep distinct from the Mozarabic Missale mixtum despite similar titles. A 1551 witness does not itself establish a substantive revision.

byzantine.rule: Audit Chrysostom, Basil and Presanctified separately. Liturgikon does not alone establish complete lections, variable hymns or calendar; identify Apostolos, Gospel, Typikon and other complementary books as applicable. Rubrical Ordo and private/solemn celebration provisions need their own scope.

alexandrian.rule: Identify which anaphoras and language layers each witness contains. Coptic and Ge’ez are separate. Establish separate lection/chant sources and local calendrical reception; notation added to a new book does not date all chant texts.

armenian.rule: Identify celebrant and minister/choir books and complementary volumes. Do not turn Latin translations or two 1677 components into successive Armenian-rite whole missals.

syriac.rule: Track common order and anaphora selection separately; identify Syriac, Garshuni and Arabic roles. A shared ancient anaphora does not prove identical later Catholic books or common approval.

east-syriac.rule: Keep ordinary/anaphoras, propers, epistle and gospel books distinct. Source reform and local implementation can have different dates. Chaldean and Syro-Malabar revision chains must not be collapsed.

western.rule: Map content actually represented: sacramentary, missal, ordinal, lectionary and gradual need not contain the same components. A pericope or preparation-prayer relationship cannot establish whole-missal ancestry. Calendar supplements are bounded components.

focused_gap_dispositions.finding: Glevaňák p.119 describes Prešov and Mukachevo using the Lviv 1905 Liturgikon. Pages 117–121 describe review of the Roman books, Gojdič’s 13 June 1943 implementation letter, interruption in 1950, Hopko’s 1966 appeal, and continued Galician-book practice. This supports historical shared-book reception and uneven reform implementation, not a unique Slovak edition or universal 1942 replacement.

inventory_followup.finding: Glevaňák (2006), p. 119, reports Prešov and Mukachevo use of the 1905 Lviv Liturgikon. This supports reception of a shared book, not a distinct Slovak edition. His account of interrupted Roman-book implementation does not establish universal adoption. SICO reports Slovak Chrysostom approval on 1997-09-14, Prot. N. 45/78. The official register reports Slovak Basil and Presanctified approval on 2004-05-29. Boháč attributes the later translations to the 1940 Grottaferrata Chrysostom and 1952 Rome Liturgikon and reports local Chrysostom introduction on 1998-02-22. Approval, source selection, publication and local use remain distinct facts.
